newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-WOMEN'S GAME OPENS UP AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WOMEN'S GAME OPENS UP AGAIN.

text.p: Steffi Graf lies injured, Monica Seles is still seeking her best form and even Swiss prodigy Martina Hingis has shown she can be beaten.
Six seeds were ousted at Wimbledon on Sunday and young pretenders as well as experienced old hands suddenly realised the world of women's tennis was opening up again.
Lindsay Davenport, seeded five, lost to an 18-year-old Czech, Denisa Chladkova, few had ever heard of and said she was feeling increasingly insecure on the court.

"They used to say we didn't have the depth in the women's game, but I know in the last year and a half I've lost to a lot more people that I didn't think in the past I would lose to," she said afterwards.
"The amount of players who could definitely win a tournament has risen -- especially this tournament," she added.

Sixth seed Amanda Coetzer of South Africa, 10th seed and former champion Conchita Martinez, Anke Huber (7), Brenda Schultz McCarthy (14) and Barbara Paulus (16) also slumped on Wimbledon's middle Sunday, usually a rest day but needed this year to clear a backlog of rain-delayed matches.
The loss of Graf, who has dominated Wimbledon for a decade, also offers hope to experienced grass-courters such as third seed Jana Novota, runner-up in 1993.
If Novotna can control the volatile temperament which saw her crash from a virtually impregnable position in the final against Graf that year, she must be among the favourites.
Novotna plays first match on Centre Court on Monday against Spaniard Gala Leon Garcia and should win.
Aranxta Sanchez Vicario, runner-up to Graf for the last two years, must also fancy her chances on Court One against Argentina's Florencia Labat.

Seles, who is keen to rediscover the success she enjoyed before a knife attack four years ago put her out of action for two years, also wants to add Wimbledon to her Grand Slam trophy collection. She faces France's Sandrine Testud in the first match on Court Three.

Meanwhile, Hingis, the youngest ever world number one at 16 and winner of the Australian Open this year, believes Graf, who is recovering from a knee operation may well have had her day at the age of 28.
"If she's going to come back for sure it's not going to be the same Steffi as she was before," Hingis said after reaching the fourth round with a 6-1 6-3 victory over Nicole Arendt on Sunday.
"You could see...that she has not been playing as well as before.
"Her career is almost over and I'm at the beginning," the Czech-born Swiss added.

Hingis has fast become the girl to beat, but she lost the French Open final to Croatian Iva Majoli when everyone expected her to win and she looked fragile in her first match at Wimbledon against Luxembourg qualifier Anne Kremer, whom she eventually overcame 6-4 6-4.
"Monica, she's always going to be a hard player and Iva, I've lost to Iva. Novotna isn't easy on this surface."

Add to the list rising stars such as Russia's Anna Kournikova, who put out the experienced Huber late on Sunday, and Mary Pierce and Hingis knows she is could be in for a tough second week in south west London.
